cultivar: Lingtou Dancong (Bai Ye), Mi Lan Xiang, Ya Shi Xiang and other Fenghuang strains
processing: Fenghuang-style dancong processing, sun-withering, overnight shaking to a medium-light oxidation, strip rolling and roasting, carried out at larger scale with more machine help; the roast is usually medium for the lowland tea and lighter for the mountain gardens.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to late April), autumn (October) and winter xue pian (December); the lower, warmer gardens give three or four pickings a year, the mountain gardens one or two.
appearance_dry: Long, even, olive-brown strips, often a little more uniform (machine-sorted) than Fenghuang mountain tea.
appearance_wet: Long yellow-green leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: Honey and florals in the manner of whichever strain it is, a lighter body than Fenghuang mountain tea, a toasty sweetness and a shorter finish; the mountain lots have more length.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. Lowland lots turn bitter quickly if steeped long; pour fast and expect six or seven good infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, often with the season but rarely with a village; spring tea is on sale from May and winter xue pian in December, sold fresh. Best within a year or two, with medium roasts keeping a little longer sealed and dry; apart from the Lingtou speciality lots it is not aged.
description:
Raoping is the other dancong county: the hills east of the Fenghuang Mountains, still in Chaozhou prefecture, where the same strains are grown at lower elevations and in far greater quantity. A large share of the tea sold around the world as Phoenix dancong is Raoping tea, and knowing that is the first step to buying dancong sensibly.

The county's tea centre is Pingxi town, home of Lingtou village and the honey-scented Lingtou Dancong cultivar that dominates its plantings, alongside Mi Lan Xiang, Ya Shi Xiang and other Fenghuang strains brought over as cuttings. Most gardens sit in warm, low hills that crop three or four times a year, which keeps prices down, but Raoping also has genuine mountain gardens around the Shuangji peaks at close to a thousand metres that make tea with real length and are sold under their own names.

Processing is the Fenghuang method at scale, sun-withering, overnight shaking, strip rolling and roasting, with more machinery and bigger batches than the hand-worked Wudong gardens. The result is a tea that is honeyed and floral according to its strain, lighter in body than the Fenghuang mountain versions, with a toasty sweetness and a finish that stops sooner. It is the tea most people are tasting when they decide whether they like dancong at all.

Brew it with the Chaozhou technique and pour fast; lowland leaf goes bitter more quickly than mountain leaf. Six or seven steeps is a fair run. The winter xue pian lots, picked in December, are light, intensely fragrant and a Raoping speciality worth buying fresh.

It is sold by year and season, cheaply and often under the plain name Phoenix dancong or a strain name with no village, which is where the mislabelling begins: Raoping tea sold honestly is good value, and Raoping tea sold as Wudong is the most common fraud in the category. Ask where it grew; a seller who answers Raoping without embarrassment is one to keep.
sources_note: The Shuangji mountain area of Raoping (Shuangji Niang Shan, around 1,000 m) is cited in Chinese sources as the county's high-elevation tea zone; production share figures are deliberately not given.
